'''Charles David Keeling''' (April 20, 1928{{snd}}June 20, 2005)<ref>
{{cite journal
|pmid=20536268
|year=2010
|last1=Harris
|first1=DC
|title=Charles David Keeling and the story of atmospheric CO2 measurements
|volume=82
|issue=19
|pages=7865–70
|doi=10.1021/ac1001492
|journal=Analytical Chemistry|bibcode=2010AnaCh..82.7865H
}}</ref><ref>
{{cite journal|pmid=16163339|year=2005|last1=Heimann|first1=M|title=Obituary: Charles David Keeling 1928–2005|volume=437|issue=7057|page=331|doi=10.1038/437331a|journal=Nature|bibcode=2005Natur.437..331H|doi-access=free}}</ref> was an American scientist whose recording of atmospheric [[carbon dioxide]] at the [[Mauna Loa Observatory]]<ref name="KaheleHanaHou">{{cite web |url= http://www.hanahou.com/pages/Magazine.asp?Action=DrawArticle&ArticleID=616&MagazineID=39 |title= Behind the Inconvenient Truth |author= Rose Kahele |work= [[Hana Hou!]] vol. 10, No. 5, October/November 2007 }}</ref> confirmed [[Svante Arrhenius]]'s proposition (1896) of the possibility of [[Human impact on the environment|anthropogenic]] contribution to the [[greenhouse effect]] and [[global warming]], by documenting the steadily rising carbon dioxide levels.  The [[Keeling Curve]] measures the progressive buildup of carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas, in the atmosphere.

==Early life and early career==
Keeling was born in [[Scranton, Pennsylvania]], to Ralph Keeling and Grace L Keeling (née Sherberne). His father, an investment banker, excited interests of [[astronomy]] in a 5-year-old Charles, while his mother instilled a lifelong love of music. He graduated with a degree in [[chemistry]] from the [[University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign|University of Illinois]] in 1948. Charles Keeling earned a PhD in [[chemistry]] from [[Northwestern University]] in 1953 under [[Malcolm Dole]], a polymer chemist. Most of Dole's graduates were going straight into the oil industry; Keeling "had trouble seeing the future this way" and had become interested in [[geology]], for which he had acquired most of the undergraduate coursework during his PhD. Keeling had applied for postdoctoral positions as a chemist almost exclusively to geology departments "west of the continental divide." He received an offer from [[Harrison Brown]] who had recently started a [[geochemistry]] department at [[California Institute of Technology]].  He was a postdoctoral fellow in [[geochemistry]] there until he joined the [[Scripps Institution of Oceanography]] in 1956, and was appointed professor of [[oceanography]] there in 1968.<ref>{{Cite journal | doi=10.1146/annurev.energy.23.1.25| doi-access=free|title = Rewards and Penalties of Monitoring the Earth| journal=[[Annual Review of Energy and the Environment]]| volume=23| pages=25–82|year = 1998|last1 = Keeling|first1 = Charles D.}}</ref>

At [[California Institute of Technology|Caltech]] he developed the first instrument able to measure carbon dioxide in atmospheric samples with consistently reliable accuracy.<ref name = "NYT01">{{cite news |title=A Scientist, His Work and a Climate Reckoning|author=Justin Gillis|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/12/22/science/earth/22carbon.html|newspaper=The New York Times|date=December 21, 2010|access-date=December 22, 2010}}</ref>  Keeling camped at [[Big Sur]] where he used his new device to measure the level of carbon dioxide and found that it had risen since the 19th century.

==Work with the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, 1958–2005==
[[Image:Mauna Loa CO2 monthly mean concentration.svg|thumbnail|right|280px|Atmospheric CO<sub>2</sub> concentrations measured at [[Mauna Loa Observatory]]: The ''[[Keeling Curve]]''.]]

century|volume=202|issue=4372|page=1109|doi=10.1126/science.202.4372.1109|journal=Science|bibcode=1978Sci...202.1109K|doi-access=}}</ref> [[Roger Revelle]], the director of the [[Scripps Institution of Oceanography]], based at [[La Jolla, California]], persuaded Keeling to continue his work there. Revelle was also one of the founders of the [[International Geophysical Year]] (IGY) in 1957–58 and Keeling received IGY funding to establish a base on [[Mauna Loa]] in Hawaii, two miles (3,000 m) above sea level.

Keeling started collecting carbon dioxide samples at the base in 1958.<ref name="KaheleHanaHou"/>  By 1960, he had established that there are strong seasonal variations in carbon dioxide levels with peak levels reached in the late northern hemisphere winter.  A reduction in carbon dioxide followed during spring and early summer each year as plant growth increased in the land-rich northern hemisphere. In 1961, Keeling produced data showing that carbon dioxide levels were rising steadily in what later became known as the "[[Keeling Curve]]".

In the early 1960s, the [[National Science Foundation]] stopped supporting his research, calling the outcome "routine". Despite this lack of interest, the Foundation used Keeling's research in its warning in 1963 of rapidly increasing amounts of heat-trapping gases. A 1965 report from [[Lyndon B. Johnson|President Johnson's]] [[President's Science Advisory Committee|Science Advisory Committee]] similarly warned of the dangers of extra heat-trapping gases, which cause the temperature of the Earth to rise.

The data collection started by Keeling and continued at Mauna Loa is the longest continuous record of atmospheric carbon dioxide in the world and is considered a reliable indicator of the global trend in the mid-level [[troposphere]]. Keeling's research showed that the atmospheric concentration of carbon dioxide grew from 315 parts per million (ppm) in 1958 to 380 (ppm) in 2005, with increases correlated to [[fossil fuel]] emissions. There has also been an increase in seasonal variation in samples from the late 20th century and early 21st century.

==Personal life==
Keeling was an enthusiastic outdoorsman who made many hiking and camping trips to the Western mountains, particularly the [[Cascade Mountains]] of [[Washington state]]. He was an active member of the [[The Wilderness Society (United States)|Wilderness Society]] for much of his life.<ref name=WS>Paul M. Keeling, "The Path to Mauna Loa", ''Wilderness''  (2008): 12-14</ref>

Keeling married Louise Barthold in 1954. They had five children, one of whom ([[Ralph Keeling]]) followed in his father's footsteps and is a climate scientist at the [[Scripps Institution of Oceanography]]. Another one of his children, Eric Keeling, currently teaches biology at SUNY New Paltz.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www3.newpaltz.edu/directory/profile/erickeeling?origin=search%3Fentity_id%3D%26first_name%3D%26last_name%3DKeeling%26phone%3D | title=SUNY New Paltz &#124; Eric Keeling |work=www3.newpaltz.edu |access-date=17 December 2022 }}</ref> Charles Keeling was also an accomplished classical pianist who almost chose a career in music. Keeling was a founding director of the [[University of California San Diego]] Madrigal Singers. He was also general chairman of the citizens committee which drafted the [[Del Mar, California|Del Mar]] General Plan (or "Community Plan") in 1975.<ref>{{cite news |author=Peter Kaye |title=Plaque honors Del Mar planners |url=http://www.utsandiego.com/news/2007/jun/24/plaque-honors-del-mar-planners/ |access-date=May 25, 2015 |work=San Diego Union-Tribune |date=June 24, 2007}}</ref>

Keeling died in 2005, aged 77, of a [[heart attack]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://scripps.ucsd.edu/news/obituary-notice-climate-science-pioneer-charles-david-keeling|title=Obituary Notice: Climate Science Pioneer: Charles David Keeling|date=June 21, 2005|access-date=June 20, 2025|publisher=[[University of California San Diego]]|website=scripps.ucsd.edu|first=Cindy|last=Clark}}</ref>

==Legacy==
* At a [[White House]] ceremony held in July 1997, Keeling was presented with a "special achievement award" from [[Vice President of the United States|Vice President]] [[Al Gore]]. Keeling was honored "for 40 years of outstanding scientific research associated with monitoring of atmospheric carbon dioxide in connection with [[Mauna Loa Observatory]]".
* The Keeling Curve is "engraved in bronze on a building at Mauna Loa and carved into a wall at the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] in Washington." It was also a chart on the wall in a classroom at [[Harvard University]] where Revelle had moved to teach in the 1960s and where among others, student [[Al Gore]] would see and "marvel" at it. In 2006, Gore featured the graph in the [[An Inconvenient Truth (book)|book]] and movie ''[[An Inconvenient Truth]]''.<ref name = "NYT01" />
* [https://scripps.ucsd.edu/people/awards/keeling/ Charles David Keeling Memorial Lecture Series] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200821060625/https://www.scripps.ucsd.edu/people/awards/keeling |date=August 21, 2020 }}, Scripps Institution of Oceanography, since 2010. 
* [https://sustainability.illinois.edu/outreach/lectures-seminars-symposia-colloquia/ Keeling Lecture], University of Illinois, since 2010. 
* The Charles David Keeling apartments at [[Revelle College]] of the [[University of California San Diego]], opened in 2011, were designed to emphasize environmental awareness and minimize ecological impact.
* ''Dr Keeling's Curve'' (2014), one-man play written by George Shea and performed by [[Mike Farrell]].<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.presstelegram.com/2014/11/04/mash-star-takes-on-global-warming-in-one-man-show-in-long-beach/ |title='M*A*S*H' star takes on global warming in one-man show in Long Beach |work=[[Press-Telegram]] |date=November 4, 2014 |access-date=December 26, 2014}}</ref>
* [https://www.kcurveprize.org''The Keeling Curve Prize'']. Multiple awards presented annually by the [https://terravivagrants.org/keeling-curve-prize-global-warming-mitigation-project/ Global Warming Mitigation Project]{{Dead link|date=September 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} since 2018.<ref>{{cite web |author1= |title=Keeling Curve Prize |url=https://www.kcurveprize.org/general-information/ |website=www.kcurveprize.org |access-date=October 5, 2019 |date= |quote=The Keeling Curve Prize rewards a diverse selection of projects reducing greenhouse gas emissions or increasing carbon uptake. |archive-date=March 22, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200322024622/https://www.kcurveprize.org/general-information }}</ref>
* On August 11, 2025, the [[minor planet]] {{mp|2005 CO|2}} was named {{LoMP|284054|284054 Keeling}} in his honor.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=(284054) Keeling = 2005 CO2|url=https://www.wgsbn-iau.org/files/Bulletins/V005/WGSBNBull_V005_019.pdf#page=9|author=[[International Astronomical Union]]|journal=WGSBN Bulletin|volume=5|number=19|page=9|date=August 11, 2025|access-date=March 18, 2026|quote=Charles David Keeling (1928–2005) was an American climatologist who developed the first reliable instrument for measuring atmospheric carbon dioxide. In 1958, at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, he began a long-term monitoring program showing by 1961 that carbon dioxide levels were rising. This ongoing record is now known as the Keeling Curve.}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=284054 Keeling (2005 CO2)|url=https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/tools/sbdb_lookup.html#/?sstr=284054&view=OPD|work=Small-Body Database Lookup|publisher=[[Jet Propulsion Laboratory]]|access-date=March 18, 2026}}</ref>

==Memberships/fellowships==
Keeling was a Guggenheim fellow at the Meteorological Institute, [[Stockholm University]] (1961–62); a guest professor at the Second Physical Institute of the [[University of Heidelberg]] (1969–70) and the Physical Institute of the [[University of Bern]] (1979–80).

He was a fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]], the American Geophysical Union, and the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]], and a member of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]].

He was a member of the commission on global pollution of the International Association of Meteorology, and scientific director of the Central CO<sub>2</sub> Calibration Laboratory of the World Meteorological Organization.
